# Workspace Rust structure and style

Status: Completed

Refactored every crate under crates/ against Google's general Rust guidance, with cohesive implementation modules, adjacent tests, consistent imports and enforced style/documentation checks. Cargo layout, runtime ownership and public entry points remain stable; post-poison behavior is explicit (D3).

## Scope

- In: All 24 workspace crates under crates/
- In: Cohesive implementation modules, explicit imports, adjacent test modules and minimum visibility
- In: Workspace formatting and Clippy enforcement
- In: Generated IA paths affected by source relocation
- Out: Chromium and Fuchsia build-system/runtime-specific rules
- Out: Third-party forks and vendor source
- Out: Product behavior, persistence formats and UI redesign

## Decision D1

Apply the general Google Rust guide in the context of an unpublished Cargo application workspace.

Why: The guide distinguishes application code from reusable libraries and labels Chromium/Fuchsia rules separately. Cargo modules, Tokio and GPUI are established project contracts.

Consequences: Keep the existing crate boundaries and Cargo directory modules; do not flatten every crate, prohibit async, or add speculative non_exhaustive/API abstractions.

## Decision D2

Keep product behavior and retained UI state ownership unchanged during the structural refactor.

Why: This work improves navigability and maintainability; mixing a redesign or migration into it would weaken review and regression evidence.

Consequences: Keep existing public re-export paths where practical, preserve source attribution and user path annotations, and regenerate affected projections. Failure-path hardening is recorded separately in D3.

## Decision D3

Treat poisoned production locks as violated invariants instead of reading their state through PoisonError::into_inner.

Why: Google's guide explicitly forbids resuming with poisoned state. A panic may interrupt a multi-field mutation, so suppressing poison makes subsequent behavior depend on an unverified state.

Consequences: Existing poison bypasses become expect calls naming the affected resource. This intentionally changes post-panic behavior to an explicit failure; normal lock operations and existing recoverable I/O/network errors retain their contracts. String formatting uses expect for its infallible writer; malformed worldgen JSON returns an error rather than panicking. Plugin catch_unwind remains a defensive isolation boundary, not a guarantee of panic safety.

## Decision D4

Use stable rustfmt for the committed formatting contract and syntax-based tests for import granularity.

Why: Google permits stable toolchains to omit unavailable rustfmt options. imports_granularity is unstable on the pinned formatter.

Consequences: rustfmt.toml fixes the 2024 style and 100-column width. The source check enforces one module per import group without requiring nightly to build, test or format the workspace. Application-specific builders, closed-world enums, shared ownership required by asynchronous lifetimes and established disambiguated framework calls remain context-dependent API decisions.

## Decision D5

Check Rustdoc links in the full handoff recipe.

Why: Moving implementation and removing unused imports can break documentation links while compilation and doctests still pass. The refactor exposed this in several modules.

Consequences: just rustdoc rejects broken links across all workspace crates, including private implementation modules, and just check runs it after formatting. This uses the stable compiler and preserves caller-supplied Rustdoc flags.

## Outcome

Completed the 24-crate structure/style refactor. Mixed boundaries now delegate to cohesive leaf modules; large stores and views split by responsibility; tests are adjacent; imports, flexible borrows and panic invariants follow the adopted application standard. Syntax-based checks and strict Rustdoc links are enforced through the repository recipes. Native verification passed. Windows/Linux builds and release publication are outside this verification result.

- Lesson: 2026-10-23: An unused public re-export inside a private feature module can still be needed only by tests. Applying production-only import fixes removed several such test seams. Guard: compile all targets after each import-cleanup pass, keep cross-feature test seams behind cfg(test), and verify the complete workspace before handoff.

- Lesson: 2026-10-23: A native build cannot prove imports used only on other platforms. Import cleanup hid the Windows credential chunk adapter and left redundant Linux/Windows pointer aliases at the facade. Guard: review inactive target-gated imports explicitly after moving modules; the credential adapter now imports chunked only on Windows, and cursor capture owns one directly qualified native alias per platform. Windows/Linux compilation was not run because only the native macOS target is installed.

- Lesson: 2026-10-23: The sandbox prevents hdiutil from creating the updater test's temporary image. The test passed with OS access; full verification uses the same access rather than skipping the test. Its assertion now includes the command, exit status, stdout and stderr so a future failure is actionable.
